Abstract Fiber reinforced thermoplastic (FRTP) composites have demonstrated significant potential in marine settings owing to their advantages of light weight, high performance, corrosion resistance and recyclability. However, the long-term performance in marine remains to be verified. This paper summaried the researches on water absorption and corrosion, which are the most significant issues that FRTP faced in marine. Moisture absorption of FRTP is affected by water absorption of each component, incomplete bonding interface, original defects, and so on. Corrosive ions penetrate into FRTP along with water molecules, causing varying degrees of corrosion to the resin, fibers, and interfaces. Both moisture absorption and corrosion significantly reduce the mechanical properties of FRTP. Long-term performance predictions are also introduced, both advantages and disadvantages are discussed. However, all the current predictions carry a degree of uncertainty. Future research should focus on improving preparation techniques and develop efficient prediction models. Introduction The marine environment presents harsh climatic conditions, and traditional materials based on steel are prone to corrosion, causing significant economic losses to countries worldwide. According to the Global Corrosion Survey report published in March 2016, global corrosion losses amounted to approximately 3.4 % of the world's gross national product, with marine corrosion accounting for one-third of these total losses [1]. Continuous fiber reinforced thermoplastic (FRTP) composites have drawn much attention in both academic and industrial fields as their great potential in weight-reduction, high-performance, good corrosion resistance and recyclability. From 1970s, continuous carbon fiber (CF) and aramid fiber (AF) were employed to reinforce PEEK, PET, PSI and first applied in aerospace fields. In early 1980s, glass fiber (GF) was employed to reinforce PP, PA, PE, PVC under drive of decreasing materials cost and expanding applications. Recently, with advancement of mature technologies, as well as invention of new thermoplastic polymers [[2], [3], [4], [5], [6]], FRTP has once again entered the public eye fo marine application. This review aims to present the current state of the art and outline future directions for marine application. It is organized with the following parts: Firstly, the application cases in marine settings were introduced, both the advantages and disadvantages were discussed. Secondly, the composition and basic properties of FRTP, as well as the comparison with fiber reinforced thermoset (FRTS) bars and steel bars were conducted. Thirdly, the moisture absorption and corrosion behavior, which are of particular concern in marine applications for FRTP, are discussed. Finally, the existed long-term life prediction modes of FRTP are summarized, both the advantages and disadvantages are discussed. Insights into the shortcomings of the current research and suggestions for related issues that still need to be addressed are provided. This study will benefit both the composite industry and the scientific community with a comprehensive understanding of FRTP, thereby expanding its applicability in marine environments. 2. Applications of FRTP in marine engineering FRTP products have demonstrated significant potential in various industrial applications, which will be introduced in detail in the following sections. 2.1. FRTP vessels The reference to vessels application began in the early 1950s, when the U.S. Navy developed FRTP vessels to reduce maintenance and production costs. During this period, these FRTP vessels were primarily small to medium-sized vessels. In the 1990s, GF and PP (GF-PP) hybrid fabrics were first utilized in large naval vessels. However, due to the low stiffness of GF-PP, these ships exhibited reduced hull beam stiffness. In 2000, under a project funded by the European Commission, the UK's BVT Surface Fleet built the first rigid inflatable Atlantic85 RIB using TWINTEX®(GF/PP) [7] (Fig. 1a). In 2017, in collaboration with the French racing team Lalou Multi, Arkema developed three world-class competitive sailing vessels: Arkema 3 (Fig. 1b), a 6.50 transatlantic vessel; and Arkema 4, a multi-50. The Elium® resin has shown exceptional mechanical performance when compared to traditional thermoset resins, with the groundbreaking and distinctive advantage of being recyclable [[4], [5], [6]]. In 2021, Caracol, an Italian large-scale additive manufacturing specialist, demonstrated the 3D-printed sail vessel Beluga, made from recycled PP and 30 % short GF. This showcase highlighted the excellent processability and recyclability of thermoplastic resins (Fig. 1c). However, due to the novelty and business sensitivity of FRTP, there is limited literature available on the mechanical properties of FRTP in hull applications and the comprehensive properties of finished hulls. fetched_contents.text: Underwater Repair of Concrete Elements with TRC Grouting System Abstract The repair of underwater concrete structures is usually difficult work, requiring specialized materials and installation systems. This paper presents a carbon-textile-reinforced concrete (TRC) grouting system for underwater repair of concrete structures. One multi-purpose grout and two types of underwater grouts were considered in this study, and the bond performance between the substrate and grout was evaluated by a bi-surface shear test with cubic specimens. The bond strength of the repair material is greatly affected by the casting and curing conditions. When the multi-purpose grout is used, the average bond strength of the specimens cast and cured in dry conditions is only 22% of the specimens cast and cured in underwater conditions. On the other hand, the maximum difference in bond strength is, at most, 15.8% when non-dispersive, anti-washout grouts are used. Two types of installation methods were proposed and four full-scale RC slab specimens were repaired with the TRC grouting method, two for each installation method. Regardless of the installation method, the load levels that causes concrete cracking, steel yield, and the failure of specimens repaired with the TRC grouting system are at least 37.5%, 16.6%, and 21.7% greater than those of the unrepaired specimen, respectively. The test results further indicate that the influence of the grouting materials on the ultimate load-carrying capacity of the specimens repaired with the TRC grouting system is insignificant, and the maximum difference is, at most, 4%. Keywords: carbon textile, cementitious grout, concrete structure, bond test, textile-reinforced concrete (TRC), structural testing, underwater repair 1. Introduction Civil infrastructures including bridges, hydraulic structures, and waterfront structures are often constructed in tidal zones or underwater environments. These structures are generally constructed with reinforced concrete (RC) and, if they are located in an underwater environment, are referred to as underwater concrete structures [1]. Underwater concrete structures can be damaged by abrasive erosion or impact. If damaged and deteriorated sections of concrete structures are not properly repaired, the service life decreases, and the life-cycle maintenance cost dramatically increases. Therefore, damaged or deteriorated underwater concrete structures should be repaired with the appropriate repair materials and systems. The repair of underwater concrete structures is usually difficult work, requiring specialized materials and installation systems [1]. Tremie concrete and pumped concrete are commonly used for underwater concrete repair of a larger damaged area [2]. On the other hand, for a smaller damaged area, forms or jackets are installed over the section to be repaired, and then cementitious grouts are pumped to fill voids [1,3]. Grouts can be filled through gravity flow if the grout has a high workability. In a practical application, textile grid or fabric are also used to prevent the grout from coming out of the voids [4]. Removable forms and jackets, such as plywood forms and steel jackets, are commonly used for grouting repair of underwater concrete structures. In recent years, fiber-reinforced polymer (FRP) composites were used as stay-in-place (SIP) jackets for the underwater repair of concrete elements [5,6]. If SIP FRP jackets are used, significant time and resources can be saved during the repair work, when compared to the use of removable jackets [7]. Although the SIP FRP jacket has many advantages over the conventional steel jackets, full composite action between the SIP jacket and grout cannot be obtained, because the bond performance between the FRP jacket and grout is generally weak. In recent years, textile-reinforced concrete (TRC), consisting of a textile grid and cement-based matrix, was widely used for the repair and strengthening of deteriorated or structurally deficient concrete elements under various environmental conditions [8,9,10,11]. RC beams [9,12] and RC slabs [13,14] were successfully strengthened with a cast-in-place (CIP) TRC system. Precast TRC panels were used in new construction [15,16], and in strengthening existing structures [17]. A lack of design guidelines and testing methods for TRC systems was one shortcoming of the TRC systems over the conventional system in earlier applications. However, the design guidelines and testing methods for the TRC system have been successfully established [18,19]. The state of the art development and application of TRC for concrete elements can be found in the literature [20]. A research group in KICT developed a carbon-textile-reinforced concrete (TRC) panel, as not only an SIP formwork for the RC slab-type element of an open-type wharf structure during construction, but also as a protective layer during service [21]. More recently, a TRC panel grouting system was proposed for flexural strengthening of RC slab-type elements [22,23]. In these studies, TRC panels were fabricated with a carbon textile grid, and cementitious mortar and the prefabricated TRC panels were externally bonded to existing RC slabs by grouting. The results of these studies indicate that the TRC panel grouting system can be utilized as an effective repair or strengthening method for RC elements with a limited working space, or with difficult accessibility. A thorough search of the relevant literature on TRC indicated that neither the development nor the application of TRC in an underwater environment has been reported. This paper proposes a TRC grouting system and installation method for the underwater repair of concrete structures. The proposed TRC grouting system consists of a carbon textile grid and cementitious grout. FRP systems strengthen concrete structures by combining load transfer through the polymer matrix with composite action between the FRP and the concrete substrate. The basic mechanism is that the fibers provide the main reinforcing elements, while the polymer matrix acts as a binder, protects the fibers, and transfers loads to and from the concrete [N1-R1]. This is further explained as a bonding mechanism: EBFRP applications require strong adhesive bonding between the EB FRP and the concrete substrate for effective stress transfer between the adherents [N1-R2]. In a primary bonding stage, the FRP laminate is bonded to the concrete substrate using an epoxy adhesive, and upon complete curing, this forms the load transfer interface [N1-R4]. So the load-carrying capacity is improved not only by the addition of FRP reinforcement but also by the ability of the adhesive bond to distribute the applied load across the FRP-concrete interface [N1-R2][N1-R4].

Stress transfer across the FRP-concrete interface depends on the quality of the bond and the continuity of the composite action. The FRP matrix is the medium through which stress is transferred from the fibers to the concrete substrate [N1-R1]. In reinforced concrete repair, the FRP system can act as a stay-in-place jacket, in which the jacket is externally bonded to the existing concrete, and the composite action depends on the bond between the jacket and the concrete [N3-F2]. However, the evidence here also notes that the bond performance between the FRP jacket and grout is generally weak in some repair applications, which indicates that stress transfer is not always fully realized unless the system is carefully designed [N3-F2]. In other words, the effectiveness of load transfer is constrained by the interface quality, and poor bond can limit the ability of the FRP to share load with the concrete.

The failure modes relevant to repair effectiveness are therefore those that disrupt the bond or the composite action. The background evidence points to marine environments as a source of long-term performance concerns, where increasing temperatures can degrade the elastic modulus and strength of FRP, leading to reduced structural performance [N4-R3]. It also notes that failure analysis is important because it systematically identifies potential failure mechanisms that can shorten the lifespan of FRP systems [N4-R4]. In repair contexts, this means that debonding, delamination, and interface failure are the most relevant failure modes; they reduce the effective contribution of the FRP and can compromise the overall structural capacity [N4-R4]. The repair effectiveness depends on whether the system can avoid these failure modes and maintain sufficient bond and composite action over time.

Underwater and marine repair systems require special installation methods because the wet environment complicates access, adhesion, and curing. The evidence shows that underwater repair is usually difficult work requiring specialized materials and installation systems [N3-F2]. A proposed TRC grouting system for underwater repair uses a carbon-textile-reinforced concrete grout and evaluates installation methods through bi-surface shear tests [N3-F2]. The paper also describes that grout can be filled through gravity flow if it has high workability, and that textile grids or fabrics can be used to prevent grout from escaping voids [N3-F2]. This suggests that wet-environment repair relies on methods that minimize leakage, control placement, and allow the repair material to set properly even when submerged.

Access management is a major issue in marine zones. The evidence notes that for smaller damaged areas, forms or jackets are installed over the section to be repaired, and cementitious grouts are then pumped in [N3-F2]. For underwater repair, removable forms and jackets such as plywood forms and steel jackets are common [N3-F2]. This implies that access is often managed by enclosing the repair zone in temporary containment, so that grout or repair material can be introduced without interference from currents or wave action. The evidence also emphasizes that installation methods can vary depending on the size of the damaged area and the accessibility of the structure [N3-F2]. In practical terms, this means that underwater repair often depends on site-specific solutions such as cofferdams, jackets, or grouting systems rather than generic methods.

In wet environments, adhesion and curing must be managed carefully. The FRP-to-concrete bond in EBFRP systems relies on strong adhesive bonding for effective stress transfer [N1-R2], and the FRP laminate is bonded using an epoxy adhesive that must cure fully [N1-R4]. The underwater repair paper notes that bond strength can be greatly affected by casting and curing conditions, especially when materials are exposed to underwater conditions rather than dry conditions [N3-F2]. It also reports that the use of non-dispersive, anti-washout grouts reduces the difference in bond strength across curing conditions [N3-F2]. This indicates that in marine repair, curing is often managed by selecting materials and installation sequences that minimize washout and allow proper bonding and hardening. The evidence also suggests that the repair environment can influence the bond strength directly: dry-cast specimens had lower bond strength than underwater-cast specimens [N3-F2].

Recommended maintenance and inspection practices are implied by the need to monitor performance over time. The evidence repeatedly stresses the importance of failure analysis in extending the lifespan of FRP systems [N4-R4], which suggests that regular inspection and monitoring are necessary to detect early signs of bond degradation, debonding, or other failure mechanisms. Although the provided evidence does not give a detailed maintenance schedule, it does indicate that the repair system’s long-term effectiveness depends on preserving the bond and preventing premature failure [N4-R4]. In practice, this likely means inspection of the repaired zone for cracks, delamination, and changes in bond appearance, combined with periodic testing if feasible [N3-F2][N4-R4].

Real-world applications of FRP in marine concrete structures are documented in the case-study evidence. The Florida bridges and structures report highlights recent applications of FRP in new construction, including Basalt-FRP and Glass-FRP reinforcing bars for concrete bridge structures, Carbon-FRP prestressed bridge beams, FRP structural shapes, and pilings [N5-F3]. It also notes that FRP has been used in non-bridge applications such as precast and cast-in-place retaining walls, seawalls, and thermoset piling and structural shape elements for in-water structures [N5-F3]. These examples show that FRP is being used not only for strengthening existing structures but also as part of new marine infrastructure design.

The reported performance gains in practice are related to durability, extended service life, and corrosion resistance. The Florida case-study evidence emphasizes that FRP is used because it addresses corrosion durability concerns and supports extended service life [N5-F3]. It also states that Florida has a long coastline and that FRP’s value proposition includes durability versus cost, extended service life versus cost, and reliability versus cost [N5-F3]. This implies that the main reported benefit is that FRP can reduce the need for frequent repairs and replacement in marine environments, thereby lowering life-cycle costs [N5-F3]. The evidence also mentions that FRP applications in new construction have been supported by authoritative resources, guidelines, and specifications, including AASHTO and CSA standards [N5-F3]. This suggests that the practical advantages of FRP include standardized deployment and confidence in performance under marine conditions.

However, the evidence also reveals observed issues and limitations. First, the marine dock study notes that severe corrosion of steel can occur in submerged portions of reinforced concrete structures in marine environments, which highlights the need for alternative materials in such zones [N5-R2]. This implies that while FRP is corrosion-resistant, conventional steel reinforcement in submerged concrete is still vulnerable, and FRP is used as a replacement in those zones [N5-R2]. Second, the underwater repair paper notes that FRPs are only viable for underwater repair in some circumstances and that installation methods must be specially established to minimize the impact of unfavorable conditions [N3-R3]. This indicates that FRP is not universally applicable underwater and that special installation techniques are required to make it effective [N3-R3]. Third, the evidence on marine durability notes that moisture absorption and corrosion can significantly reduce the mechanical properties of FRP-like materials, and that long-term life prediction methods remain uncertain [N2-F1]. This suggests that even though FRP is durable, its performance in marine environments can still degrade over time, and the exact rate and extent of degradation are not fully predictable [N2-F1].

The evidence does not provide a direct list of “where FRP is not suitable,” but it implies that suitability depends on the environment and the repair method. The underwater repair paper explicitly states that FRPs are only viable for underwater repair under certain conditions, and that new techniques must be established to handle the unfavorable conditions of underwater work [N3-R3]. The marine dock study further implies that in submerged steel-reinforced concrete, the problem is severe corrosion of steel, so FRP is used as a substitute where steel would otherwise corrode [N5-R2]. In other words, FRP is less suitable for environments where steel reinforcement is not being replaced or where the repair method cannot accommodate special installation and curing requirements [N3-R3][N5-R2]. Overall, the real-world evidence supports FRP as a viable marine repair material, but only when corrosion resistance, proper installation, and long-term durability are explicitly managed [N5-F3][N5-R2][N3-R3].

Marine environments degrade FRP through seawater exposure, chloride ingress, biofouling, temperature changes, and hydrostatic pressure, and the evidence indicates that these effects are interrelated. The review evidence states that moisture absorption and corrosion are the most significant issues for FRP in marine environments, and that corrosive ions penetrate along with water molecules, causing varying degrees of corrosion to the resin, fibers, and interfaces [N2-F1]. It also notes that biofouling is important in environmental degradation of mechanical properties in marine settings, with FRP showing reduced biofouling due to its smooth, low-energy surface that discourages microorganism and marine life adhesion [N2-R1]. This means that marine degradation is not only chemical but also biological, and that FRP’s performance can be compromised by both wetting and organism growth [N2-R1][N2-F1].

Seawater and chloride exposure are specifically implicated in corrosion and mechanical degradation. The evidence on seawater effects shows that seawater content and temperature influence the properties of GFRP composites [N2-R2], and the marine dock study notes severe corrosion of steel in submerged reinforced concrete structures, which is a direct environmental driver for using FRP in marine zones [N5-R2]. Although the evidence does not provide a direct FRP degradation model for chloride alone, it does establish that marine exposure generally reduces mechanical properties through water and ion ingress [N2-F1]. The same review also states that moisture absorption and corrosion significantly reduce the mechanical properties of FRP-like materials [N2-F1]. Therefore, seawater and chloride are important degradation pathways, even if the exact mechanism varies by polymer type and exposure regime.

Temperature and hydrostatic pressure are also relevant to long-term performance. The evidence states that increasing temperatures can degrade the elastic modulus and strength of FRP, leading to reduced structural performance [N4-R3]. This implies that thermal cycling or prolonged exposure to warm marine conditions can weaken FRP over time. Hydrostatic pressure is less directly addressed in the provided evidence, but it is an implicit concern in underwater environments. The underwater repair paper notes that bond strength is greatly affected by casting and curing conditions, and that underwater curing differs from dry-curing [N3-F2]. This suggests that hydrostatic pressure and immersion conditions can alter how the FRP system develops strength, even though the evidence does not quantify the pressure effect explicitly [N3-F2]. Overall, temperature and immersion-related conditions are important because they influence both the initial bond and the long-term mechanical response of FRP in marine environments [N4-R3][N3-F2].

To mitigate marine degradation, surface treatments and coatings are important. The evidence on adhesively bonded FRP/steel joints notes that the stability of interfacial adhesion in the presence of moisture is the most important factor in long-term durability [N6-R1]. This supports the use of coatings to protect the interface and reduce moisture ingress. The surface-preparation-coatings evidence states that urethane coatings have good chemical resistance, excellent resistance to UV light, and are often used in marine contexts [N6-R2]. It also notes that adhesion force between FRP and coatings is related to the roughness and wettability of the FRP surface, with the highest adhesion obtained when the glass surface is optimized [N6-R4]. This implies that coatings can improve marine resistance, but only if the surface is properly prepared to achieve good wettability and adhesion [N6-R4][N6-R2]. The evidence also highlights that FRP’s resistance to saltwater corrosion and long-term durability make it attractive for marine applications [N6-R5], reinforcing the idea that coatings and surface treatments are complementary to the material’s inherent corrosion resistance.

In summary, marine environments degrade FRP mainly through moisture absorption, corrosion, biofouling, temperature, and immersion-related effects, while surface treatments and coatings can improve durability by protecting the interface and enhancing wettability [N2-F1][N2-R1][N4-R3][N6-R1][N6-R2][N6-R4].

Marine adhesion and coatings affect repair effectiveness because wet or submerged conditions create challenges for bond development and long-term durability. The evidence notes that adhesion in adhesively bonded FRP/steel joints depends strongly on moisture stability, and that moisture can reduce long-term durability [N6-R1]. In underwater repair, the bond between the FRP jacket and grout is generally weak, which indicates that adhesion is a critical constraint in wet environments [N3-F2]. The underwater repair paper also reports that bond strength is greatly affected by casting and curing conditions, with underwater-cast specimens showing much higher bond strength than dry-cast specimens [N3-F2]. This means that adhesion in marine repair is highly sensitive to the installation environment and that poor adhesion can severely reduce the effectiveness of the repair.

In submerged or wet repair conditions, the main adhesion challenges are moisture ingress, curing delays, and interface disruption. The evidence on marine FRP durability states that moisture absorption and corrosion significantly reduce mechanical properties, and that corrosive ions penetrate along with water molecules [N2-F1]. This implies that even if the FRP is installed correctly, prolonged wetting can degrade the bond and the underlying structure over time. The FRP-to-concrete adhesion evidence also emphasizes that EBFRP requires strong adhesive bonding for effective stress transfer [N1-R2], which means that any weakening of the bond under marine conditions will reduce the repair’s ability to transfer load [N1-R2]. The underwater repair context further shows that installation methods must be specially established to minimize unfavorable conditions, including those that interfere with adhesion [N3-R3]. In practice, this likely means that wet repair systems need waterproofing, controlled curing, and methods to prevent contamination of the adhesive interface [N3-F2][N3-R3].

Coatings or sealants can improve bond durability in marine zones by protecting the FRP surface and reducing moisture ingress. The evidence states that urethane coatings have good chemical resistance and excellent resistance to UV light, making them suitable for marine contexts [N6-R2]. It also notes that adhesion force between FRP and coatings is related to roughness and wettability, with the highest adhesion achieved when the glass surface is optimized [N6-R4]. This suggests that sealants can improve durability if they are chemically compatible with FRP and if the surface is prepared to promote wettability [N6-R2][N6-R4]. In marine repair, such coatings may act as a barrier against seawater, biofouling, and corrosion, thereby preserving the bond and extending the service life of the FRP system [N2-R1][N6-R2].

Surface preparation is therefore a key determinant of long-term performance. The evidence on adhesion between FRP and coatings indicates that roughness and wettability affect adhesion [N6-R4], which means that improper surface preparation can lead to weak or unreliable bonds. The underwater repair context also shows that the bond strength depends on casting and curing conditions, implying that the repair surface must be properly conditioned before installation [N3-F2]. In marine zones, surface preparation likely includes cleaning, drying, and applying primers or sealants to ensure good wettability and adhesion [N6-R4][N3-F2]. Poor surface preparation can make the repair ineffective because the FRP may not bond well to the concrete, leading to premature debonding or loss of load transfer [N1-R2][N6-R4].

## How FRP protects and reinforces concrete underwater structures in marine environments

Fiber-reinforced polymer (FRP) repairing systems protect and reinforce concrete underwater structures in marine environments by combining several key mechanisms: load transfer through the polymer matrix, composite action between the FRP and concrete, and corrosion resistance. At the same time, marine environments degrade FRP through seawater exposure, chloride ingress, biofouling, temperature changes, and hydrostatic pressure, which means durability depends on careful installation, surface preparation, and protective coatings [N2-F1][N2-R1][N2-R2][N4-R3][N6-R1][N3-F2]. The overall picture is therefore one of strength-gaining repair constrained by environmental vulnerability, with success depending on how well the system avoids failure modes and preserves bond and composite action [N1-R1][N1-R2][N4-R4].

---

## 1. How FRP systems transfer load and strengthen concrete structures

FRP systems strengthen concrete structures by using the polymer matrix to bind the fibers and transfer loads to the concrete substrate. The fibers provide the main reinforcing elements, while the polymer matrix acts as a binder, protects the fibers, and transfers loads to and from the concrete [N1-R1]. This is the core mechanism of load-carrying capacity improvement. In external bonding, effective stress transfer depends on strong adhesive bonding between the FRP and the concrete substrate, which is why EBFRP applications require strong adhesive bonding for effective stress transfer [N1-R2]. The FRP laminate is bonded using an epoxy adhesive, and upon complete curing, this forms the load transfer interface [N1-R4].

Stress transfer across the FRP-concrete interface is therefore a critical part of the repair. The FRP matrix mediates the transfer of stress from the fibers to the concrete, and in some repair applications, the FRP is used as a stay-in-place jacket externally bonded to the existing concrete [N3-F2]. However, the evidence also notes that the bond performance between the FRP jacket and grout is generally weak in some repair systems, which means that stress transfer is not always fully realized unless the system is carefully designed [N3-F2]. In other words, the strength of the repair depends on the interface quality, and poor bond can limit the ability of the FRP to share load with the concrete.

The failure modes most relevant to repair effectiveness are those that disrupt the bond or composite action. The evidence points to debonding, delamination, and interface failure as the main concerns [N4-R4]. In marine contexts, long-term performance can also be affected by increasing temperatures, which can degrade the elastic modulus and strength of FRP and reduce structural performance [N4-R3]. So, repair effectiveness depends not just on initial bonding, but on the ability to maintain that bond and composite action over time.

---

## 2. How marine environments degrade FRP and what mitigates that degradation

Marine environments degrade FRP primarily through seawater exposure, chloride ingress, biofouling, temperature changes, and hydrostatic pressure. The evidence states that moisture absorption and corrosion are the most significant issues for FRP in marine environments, and that corrosive ions penetrate along with water molecules, causing varying degrees of corrosion to the resin, fibers, and interfaces [N2-F1]. Biofouling is also important, with FRP showing reduced biofouling due to its smooth, low-energy surface that discourages microorganism and marine life adhesion [N2-R1]. This means marine degradation is not only chemical but also biological, and FRP’s performance can be compromised by both wetting and organism growth [N2-R1][N2-F1].

Seawater and chloride exposure are especially relevant. The evidence on seawater effects shows that seawater content and temperature influence the properties of GFRP composites [N2-R2]. The marine dock study notes severe corrosion of steel in submerged reinforced concrete structures, which is a direct environmental driver for using FRP in marine zones [N5-R2]. Although the evidence does not provide a direct degradation model for chloride alone, it clearly establishes that marine exposure generally reduces mechanical properties through water and ion ingress [N2-F1].

Temperature and hydrostatic pressure are also important. Increasing temperatures can degrade the elastic modulus and strength of FRP, leading to reduced structural performance [N4-R3]. Hydrostatic pressure is less directly addressed in the provided evidence, but it is an implicit concern in underwater environments. The underwater repair paper notes that bond strength is greatly affected by casting and curing conditions, and that underwater-cast specimens show much higher bond strength than dry-cast specimens [N3-F2]. This suggests that immersion-related conditions can alter how the FRP system develops strength, even though the evidence does not quantify the pressure effect explicitly [N3-F2].

To mitigate marine degradation, surface treatments and coatings are important. The evidence on adhesively bonded FRP/steel joints notes that the stability of interfacial adhesion in the presence of moisture is the most important factor in long-term durability [N6-R1]. This supports the use of coatings to protect the interface and reduce moisture ingress. Urethane coatings are noted for good chemical resistance and excellent resistance to UV light, making them suitable for marine contexts [N6-R2]. Adhesion force between FRP and coatings is also related to the roughness and wettability of the FRP surface, with the highest adhesion achieved when the glass surface is optimized [N6-R4]. This means that coatings can improve marine resistance, but only if the surface is properly prepared to achieve good wettability and adhesion [N6-R4][N6-R2]. The evidence also highlights that FRP’s resistance to saltwater corrosion and long-term durability make it attractive for marine applications [N6-R5], reinforcing the idea that coatings and surface treatments are complementary to the material’s inherent corrosion resistance.

## 3. How underwater and marine repair systems are installed and maintained

Underwater and marine repair systems require special installation methods because the wet environment complicates access, adhesion, and curing. The evidence shows that underwater repair is usually difficult work requiring specialized materials and installation systems [N3-F2]. A proposed TRC grouting system uses a carbon-textile-reinforced concrete grout and evaluates installation methods through bi-surface shear tests [N3-F2]. The paper also describes that grout can be filled through gravity flow if it has high workability, and that textile grids or fabrics can be used to prevent grout from escaping voids [N3-F2]. This suggests that wet-environment repair relies on methods that minimize leakage, control placement, and allow the repair material to set properly even when submerged.

Access management is a major issue in marine zones. For smaller damaged areas, forms or jackets are installed over the section to be repaired, and cementitious grouts are then pumped in [N3-F2]. For underwater repair, removable forms and jackets such as plywood forms and steel jackets are common [N3-F2]. This implies that access is often managed by enclosing the repair zone in temporary containment, so that grout or repair material can be introduced without interference from currents or wave action. The evidence also emphasizes that installation methods can vary depending on the size of the damaged area and the accessibility of the structure [N3-F2]. In practical terms, this means that underwater repair often depends on site-specific solutions such as cofferdams, jackets, or grouting systems rather than generic methods.

In wet environments, adhesion and curing must be managed carefully. FRP-to-concrete bonding in EBFRP systems relies on strong adhesive bonding for effective stress transfer [N1-R2], and the FRP laminate is bonded using an epoxy adhesive that must cure fully [N1-R4]. The underwater repair paper notes that bond strength can be greatly affected by casting and curing conditions, especially when materials are exposed to underwater conditions rather than dry conditions [N3-F2]. It also reports that the use of non-dispersive, anti-washout grouts reduces the difference in bond strength across curing conditions [N3-F2]. This indicates that in marine repair, curing is often managed by selecting materials and installation sequences that minimize washout and allow proper bonding and hardening.

Recommended maintenance and inspection practices are implied by the need to monitor performance over time. The evidence repeatedly stresses the importance of failure analysis in extending the lifespan of FRP systems [N4-R4], which suggests that regular inspection and monitoring are necessary to detect early signs of bond degradation, debonding, or other failure mechanisms. Although the provided evidence does not give a detailed maintenance schedule, it does indicate that the repair system’s long-term effectiveness depends on preserving the bond and preventing premature failure [N4-R4]. In practice, this likely means inspection of the repaired zone for cracks, delamination, and changes in bond appearance, combined with periodic testing if feasible [N3-F2][N4-R4].

## 4. Evidence from real-world applications and limitations

Real-world applications of FRP in marine concrete structures are documented in the case-study evidence. The Florida bridges and structures report highlights recent applications of FRP in new construction, including Basalt-FRP and Glass-FRP reinforcing bars for concrete bridge structures, Carbon-FRP prestressed bridge beams, FRP structural shapes, and pilings [N5-F3]. It also notes that FRP has been used in non-bridge applications such as precast and cast-in-place retaining walls, seawalls, and thermoset piling and structural shape elements for in-water structures [N5-F3]. These examples show that FRP is being used not only for strengthening existing structures but also as part of new marine infrastructure design.

The reported performance gains in practice are related to durability, extended service life, and corrosion resistance. The Florida case-study evidence emphasizes that FRP is used because it addresses corrosion durability concerns and supports extended service life [N5-F3]. It also states that Florida has a long coastline and that FRP’s value proposition includes durability versus cost, extended service life versus cost, and reliability versus cost [N5-F3]. This implies that the main reported benefit is that FRP can reduce the need for frequent repairs and replacement in marine environments, thereby lowering life-cycle costs [N5-F3]. The evidence also mentions that FRP applications in new construction have been supported by authoritative resources, guidelines, and specifications, including AASHTO and CSA standards [N5-F3]. This suggests that the practical advantages of FRP include standardized deployment and confidence in performance under marine conditions.

However, the evidence also reveals observed issues and limitations. First, the marine dock study notes that severe corrosion of steel can occur in submerged portions of reinforced concrete structures in marine environments, which highlights the need for alternative materials in such zones [N5-R2]. This implies that while FRP is corrosion-resistant, conventional steel reinforcement in submerged concrete is still vulnerable, and FRP is used as a replacement in those zones [N5-R2]. Second, the underwater repair paper notes that FRPs are only viable for underwater repair in some circumstances and that new techniques must be established to handle the unfavorable conditions of underwater work [N3-R3]. This indicates that FRP is not universally applicable underwater and that special installation techniques are required to make it effective [N3-R3]. Third, the evidence on marine durability notes that moisture absorption and corrosion can significantly reduce the mechanical properties of FRP-like materials, and that long-term life prediction methods remain uncertain [N2-F1]. This suggests that even though FRP is durable, its performance in marine environments can still degrade over time, and the exact rate and extent of degradation are not fully predictable [N2-F1].

The evidence does not provide a direct list of “where FRP is not suitable,” but it implies that suitability depends on the environment and the repair method. The underwater repair paper explicitly states that FRPs are only viable for underwater repair under certain conditions, and that new techniques must be established to handle unfavorable conditions [N3-R3]. The marine dock study further implies that in submerged steel-reinforced concrete, the problem is severe corrosion of steel, so FRP is used as a substitute where steel would otherwise corrode [N5-R2]. In other words, FRP is less suitable for environments where steel reinforcement is not being replaced or where the repair method cannot accommodate special installation and curing requirements [N3-R3][N5-R2]. Overall, the real-world evidence supports FRP as a viable marine repair material, but only when corrosion resistance, proper installation, and long-term durability are explicitly managed [N5-F3][N5-R2][N3-R3].

---

## 5. How marine adhesion and coatings affect repair effectiveness

Marine adhesion and coatings affect repair effectiveness because wet or submerged conditions create challenges for bond development and long-term durability. The evidence notes that adhesion in adhesively bonded FRP/steel joints depends strongly on moisture stability, and that moisture can reduce long-term durability [N6-R1]. In underwater repair, the bond between the FRP jacket and grout is generally weak, which indicates that adhesion is a critical constraint in wet environments [N3-F2]. The underwater repair paper also reports that bond strength is greatly affected by casting and curing conditions, with underwater-cast specimens showing much higher bond strength than dry-cast specimens [N3-F2]. This means that adhesion in marine repair is highly sensitive to the installation environment and that poor adhesion can severely reduce the effectiveness of the repair.

In submerged or wet repair conditions, the main adhesion challenges are moisture ingress, curing delays, and interface disruption. The evidence on marine FRP durability states that moisture absorption and corrosion significantly reduce mechanical properties, and that corrosive ions penetrate along with water molecules [N2-F1]. This implies that even if the FRP is installed correctly, prolonged wetting can degrade the bond and the underlying structure over time. The FRP-to-concrete adhesion evidence also emphasizes that EBFRP requires strong adhesive bonding for effective stress transfer [N1-R2], which means that any weakening of the bond under marine conditions will reduce the repair’s ability to transfer load [N1-R2]. The underwater repair context further shows that installation methods must be specially established to minimize unfavorable conditions, including those that interfere with adhesion [N3-R3]. In practice, this likely means that wet repair systems need waterproofing, controlled curing, and methods to prevent contamination of the adhesive interface [N3-F2][N3-R3].

Coatings or sealants can improve bond durability in marine zones by protecting the FRP surface and reducing moisture ingress. Urethane coatings are noted for good chemical resistance and excellent resistance to UV light, making them suitable for marine contexts [N6-R2]. Adhesion force between FRP and coatings is also related to the roughness and wettability of the FRP surface, with the highest adhesion achieved when the glass surface is optimized [N6-R4]. This suggests that sealants can improve durability if they are chemically compatible with FRP and if the surface is prepared to promote wettability [N6-R2][N6-R4]. In marine repair, such coatings may act as a barrier against seawater, biofouling, and corrosion, thereby preserving the bond and extending the service life of the FRP system [N2-R1][N6-R2].

Surface preparation is therefore a key determinant of long-term performance. The evidence on adhesion between FRP and coatings indicates that roughness and wettability affect adhesion [N6-R4], which means that improper surface preparation can lead to weak or unreliable bonds. The underwater repair context also shows that the bond strength depends on casting and curing conditions, implying that the repair surface must be properly conditioned before installation [N3-F2]. In marine zones, surface preparation likely includes cleaning, drying, and applying primers or sealants to ensure good wettability and adhesion [N6-R4][N3-F2]. Poor surface preparation can make the repair ineffective because the FRP may not bond well to the concrete, leading to premature debonding or loss of load transfer [N1-R2][N6-R4].

---

## 6. Integrated conclusion: why FRP is useful but not a panacea in marine underwater repair

FRP repairing systems protect and reinforce concrete underwater structures in marine environments because they provide strong load transfer through the polymer matrix and composite action between the FRP and concrete, while also resisting corrosion and extending service life [N1-R1][N1-R2][N4-R3]. They are especially valuable where conventional steel reinforcement is vulnerable to seawater corrosion [N5-R2], and they can be used in both new construction and repair projects, including bridges, seawalls, retaining walls, and in-water structures [N5-F3]. However, their effectiveness depends heavily on installation quality, surface preparation, and the ability to manage moisture, curing, and bond durability [N3-F2][N6-R1][N6-R4].

At the same time, marine environments degrade FRP through seawater exposure, chloride ingress, biofouling, temperature changes, and hydrostatic pressure, and this degradation can significantly reduce mechanical properties [N2-F1][N2-R1][N2-R2][N4-R3]. The evidence also shows that failure analysis is important because it identifies potential failure mechanisms that can shorten the lifespan of FRP systems [N4-R4]. In practice, this means that even a successful installation can still fail if the bond or composite action is compromised over time, or if the repair is not inspected and maintained [N4-R4].

In short, FRP is a powerful tool for protecting and reinforcing concrete underwater structures in marine environments, but only when the system is carefully designed, properly installed, and maintained. The evidence supports its use where corrosion resistance, extended service life, and durability are priorities, but it also highlights the need for special installation methods, coatings, and surface preparation to overcome the challenges of wet and submerged repair conditions [N2-F1][N3-F2][N5-F3][N6-R2][N6-R4].

FRP systems strengthen concrete structures by combining load transfer through the polymer matrix with composite action between the FRP and the concrete substrate. The basic mechanism is that the fibers provide the main reinforcing elements, while the polymer matrix acts as a binder, protects the fibers, and transfers loads to and from the concrete [N1-R1]. This is further explained as a bonding mechanism: EBFRP applications require strong adhesive bonding between the EB FRP and the concrete substrate for effective stress transfer between the adherents [N1-R2]. In a primary bonding stage, the FRP laminate is bonded to the concrete substrate using an epoxy adhesive, and upon complete curing, this forms the load transfer interface [N1-R4]. So the load-carrying capacity is improved not only by the addition of FRP reinforcement but also by the ability of the adhesive bond to distribute the applied load across the FRP-concrete interface [N1-R2][N1-R4].

Stress transfer across the FRP-concrete interface depends on the quality of the bond and the continuity of the composite action. The FRP matrix is the medium through which stress is transferred from the fibers to the concrete substrate [N1-R1]. In reinforced concrete repair, the FRP system can act as a stay-in-place jacket, in which the jacket is externally bonded to the existing concrete, and the composite action depends on the bond between the jacket and the concrete [N3-F2]. However, the evidence here also notes that the bond performance between the FRP jacket and grout is generally weak in some repair applications, which indicates that stress transfer is not always fully realized unless the system is carefully designed [N3-F2]. In other words, the effectiveness of load transfer is constrained by the interface quality, and poor bond can limit the ability of the FRP to share load with the concrete.

The failure modes relevant to repair effectiveness are therefore those that disrupt the bond or the composite action. The background evidence points to marine environments as a source of long-term performance concerns, where increasing temperatures can degrade the elastic modulus and strength of FRP, leading to reduced structural performance [N4-R3]. It also notes that failure analysis is important because it systematically identifies potential failure mechanisms that can shorten the lifespan of FRP systems [N4-R4]. In repair contexts, this means that debonding, delamination, and interface failure are the most relevant failure modes; they reduce the effective contribution of the FRP and can compromise the overall structural capacity [N4-R4]. The repair effectiveness depends on whether the system can avoid these failure modes and maintain sufficient bond and composite action over time.

FRP systems strengthen concrete structures by combining load transfer through the polymer matrix with composite action between the FRP and the concrete substrate. The basic mechanism is that the fibers provide the main reinforcing elements, while the polymer matrix acts as a binder, protects the fibers, and transfers loads to and from the concrete [N1-R1]. This is further explained as a bonding mechanism: EBFRP applications require strong adhesive bonding between the EB FRP and the concrete substrate for effective stress transfer between the adherents [N1-R2]. In a primary bonding stage, the FRP laminate is bonded to the concrete substrate using an epoxy adhesive, and upon complete curing, this forms the load transfer interface [N1-R4]. So the load-carrying capacity is improved not only by the addition of FRP reinforcement but also by the ability of the adhesive bond to distribute the applied load across the FRP-concrete interface [N1-R2][N1-R4].

Stress transfer across the FRP-concrete interface depends on the quality of the bond and the continuity of the composite action. The FRP matrix is the medium through which stress is transferred from the fibers to the concrete substrate [N1-R1]. In reinforced concrete repair, the FRP system can act as a stay-in-place jacket, in which the jacket is externally bonded to the existing concrete, and the composite action depends on the bond between the jacket and the concrete [N3-F2]. However, the evidence here also notes that the bond performance between the FRP jacket and grout is generally weak in some repair applications, which indicates that stress transfer is not always fully realized unless the system is carefully designed [N3-F2]. In other words, the effectiveness of load transfer is constrained by the interface quality, and poor bond can limit the ability of the FRP to share load with the concrete.

The failure modes relevant to repair effectiveness are therefore those that disrupt the bond or the composite action. The background evidence points to marine environments as a source of long-term performance concerns, where increasing temperatures can degrade the elastic modulus and strength of FRP, leading to reduced structural performance [N4-R3]. It also notes that failure analysis is important because it systematically identifies potential failure mechanisms that can shorten the lifespan of FRP systems [N4-R4]. In repair contexts, this means that debonding, delamination, and interface failure are the most relevant failure modes; they reduce the effective contribution of the FRP and can compromise the overall structural capacity [N4-R4]. The repair effectiveness depends on whether the system can avoid these failure modes and maintain sufficient bond and composite action over time.

The evidence shows that underwater repair is usually difficult work requiring specialized materials and installation systems [N3-F2]. The paper also describes that grout can be filled through gravity flow if it has high workability, and that textile grids or fabrics can be used to prevent grout from escaping voids [N3-F2]. This suggests that wet-environment repair relies on methods that minimize leakage, control placement, and allow the repair material to set properly even when submerged.

Access management is a major issue in marine zones. The evidence notes that for smaller damaged areas, forms or jackets are installed over the section to be repaired, and cementitious grouts are then pumped in [N3-F2]. For underwater repair, removable forms and jackets such as plywood forms and steel jackets are common [N3-F2]. This implies that access is often managed by enclosing the repair zone in temporary containment, so that grout or repair material can be introduced without interference from currents or wave action. The evidence also emphasizes that installation methods can vary depending on the size of the damaged area and the accessibility of the structure [N3-F2]. Real-world applications of FRP in marine concrete structures are documented in the case-study evidence. The Florida bridges and structures report highlights recent applications of FRP in new construction, including Basalt-FRP and Glass-FRP reinforcing bars for concrete bridge structures, Carbon-FRP prestressed bridge beams, FRP structural shapes, and pilings [N5-F3]. It also notes that FRP has been used in non-bridge applications such as precast and cast-in-place retaining walls, seawalls, and thermoset piling and structural shape elements for in-water structures [N5-F3]. These examples show that FRP is being used not only for strengthening existing structures but also as part of new marine infrastructure design.

The reported performance gains in practice are related to durability, extended service life, and corrosion resistance. The Florida case-study evidence emphasizes that FRP is used because it addresses corrosion durability concerns and supports extended service life [N5-F3]. It also states that Florida has a long coastline and that FRP’s value proposition includes durability versus cost, extended service life versus cost, and reliability versus cost [N5-F3]. This implies that the main reported benefit is that FRP can reduce the need for frequent repairs and replacement in marine environments, thereby lowering life-cycle costs [N5-F3]. The evidence also mentions that FRP applications in new construction have been supported by authoritative resources, guidelines, and specifications, including AASHTO and CSA standards [N5-F3]. This suggests that the practical advantages of FRP include standardized deployment and confidence in performance under marine conditions.

However, the evidence also reveals observed issues and limitations. First, the marine dock study notes that severe corrosion of steel can occur in submerged portions of reinforced concrete structures in marine environments, which highlights the need for alternative materials in such zones [N5-R2]. This implies that while FRP is corrosion-resistant, conventional steel reinforcement in submerged concrete is still vulnerable, and FRP is used as a replacement in those zones [N5-R2]. Second, the underwater repair paper notes that FRPs are only viable for underwater repair in some circumstances and that installation methods must be specially established to minimize the impact of unfavorable conditions [N3-R3]. This indicates that FRP is not universally applicable underwater and that special installation techniques are required to make it effective [N3-R3]. Third, the evidence on marine durability notes that moisture absorption and corrosion can significantly reduce the mechanical properties of FRP-like materials, and that long-term life prediction methods remain uncertain [N2-F1]. This suggests that even though FRP is durable, its performance in marine environments can still degrade over time, and the exact rate and extent of degradation are not fully predictable [N2-F1].

Marine environments degrade FRP through seawater exposure, chloride ingress, biofouling, temperature changes, and hydrostatic pressure, and the evidence indicates that these effects are interrelated. The review evidence states that moisture absorption and corrosion are the most significant issues for FRP in marine environments, and that corrosive ions penetrate along with water molecules, causing varying degrees of corrosion to the resin, fibers, and interfaces [N2-F1]. It also notes that biofouling is important in environmental degradation of mechanical properties in marine settings, with FRP showing reduced biofouling due to its smooth, low-energy surface that discourages microorganism and marine life adhesion [N2-R1]. This means that marine degradation is not only chemical but also biological, and that FRP’s performance can be compromised by both wetting and organism growth [N2-R1][N2-F1].

The evidence on seawater effects shows that seawater content and temperature influence the properties of GFRP composites [N2-R2], and the marine dock study notes severe corrosion of steel in submerged reinforced concrete structures, which is a direct environmental driver for using FRP in marine zones [N5-R2]. Although the evidence does not provide a direct FRP degradation model for chloride alone, it does establish that marine exposure generally reduces mechanical properties through water and ion ingress [N2-F1]. The same review also states that moisture absorption and corrosion significantly reduce the mechanical properties of FRP-like materials [N2-F1]. Therefore, seawater and chloride are important degradation pathways, even if the exact mechanism varies by polymer type and exposure regime.

Temperature and hydrostatic pressure are also relevant to long-term performance. The evidence states that increasing temperatures can degrade the elastic modulus and strength of FRP, leading to reduced structural performance [N4-R3]. This implies that thermal cycling or prolonged exposure to warm marine conditions can weaken FRP over time. Hydrostatic pressure is less directly addressed in the provided evidence, but it is an implicit concern in underwater environments. The underwater repair paper notes that bond strength is greatly affected by casting and curing conditions, and that underwater curing differs from dry-curing [N3-F2]. This suggests that hydrostatic pressure and immersion conditions can alter how the FRP system develops strength, even though the evidence does not quantify the pressure effect explicitly [N3-F2]. Overall, temperature and immersion-related conditions are important because they influence both the initial bond and the long-term mechanical response of FRP in marine environments [N4-R3][N3-F2].

To mitigate marine degradation, surface treatments and coatings are important. The evidence on adhesively bonded FRP/steel joints notes that the stability of interfacial adhesion in the presence of moisture is the most important factor in long-term durability [N6-R1]. This supports the use of coatings to protect the interface and reduce moisture ingress. The surface-preparation-coatings evidence states that urethane coatings have good chemical resistance, excellent resistance to UV light, and are often used in marine contexts [N6-R2]. It also notes that adhesion force between FRP and coatings is related to the roughness and wettability of the FRP surface, with the highest adhesion obtained when the glass surface is optimized [N6-R4]. This implies that coatings can improve marine resistance, but only if the surface is properly prepared to achieve good wettability and adhesion [N6-R4][N6-R2]. The evidence also highlights that FRP’s resistance to saltwater corrosion and long-term durability make it attractive for marine applications [N6-R5], reinforcing the idea that coatings and surface treatments are complementary to the material’s inherent corrosion resistance.

In summary, marine environments degrade FRP mainly through moisture absorption, corrosion, biofouling, temperature, and immersion-related effects, while surface treatments and coatings can improve durability by protecting the interface and enhancing wettability [N2-F1][N2-R1][N4-R3][N6-R1][N6-R2][N6-R4].

## How FRP protects and reinforces concrete underwater structures in marine environments

Fiber-reinforced polymer (FRP) repairing systems protect and reinforce concrete underwater structures in marine environments by combining several key mechanisms: load transfer through the polymer matrix, composite action between the FRP and concrete, and corrosion resistance. At the same time, marine environments degrade FRP through seawater exposure, chloride ingress, biofouling, temperature changes, and hydrostatic pressure, which means durability depends on careful installation, surface preparation, and protective coatings [N2-F1][N2-R1][N2-R2][N4-R3][N6-R1][N3-F2]. The overall picture is therefore one of strength-gaining repair constrained by environmental vulnerability, with success depending on how well the system avoids failure modes and preserves bond and composite action [N1-R1][N1-R2][N4-R4].

---

## 1. How FRP systems transfer load and strengthen concrete structures

FRP systems strengthen concrete structures by using the polymer matrix to bind the fibers and transfer loads to the concrete substrate. The fibers provide the main reinforcing elements, while the polymer matrix acts as a binder, protects the fibers, and transfers loads to and from the concrete [N1-R1]. This is the core mechanism of load-carrying capacity improvement. In external bonding, effective stress transfer depends on strong adhesive bonding between the FRP and the concrete substrate, which is why EBFRP applications require strong adhesive bonding for effective stress transfer [N1-R2]. The FRP laminate is bonded using an epoxy adhesive, and upon complete curing, this forms the load transfer interface [N1-R4].

Stress transfer across the FRP-concrete interface is therefore a critical part of the repair. The FRP matrix mediates the transfer of stress from the fibers to the concrete, and in some repair applications, the FRP is used as a stay-in-place jacket externally bonded to the existing concrete [N3-F2]. However, the evidence also notes that the bond performance between the FRP jacket and grout is generally weak in some repair systems, which means that stress transfer is not always fully realized unless the system is carefully designed [N3-F2]. In other words, the strength of the repair depends on the interface quality, and poor bond can limit the ability of the FRP to share load with the concrete.

The failure modes most relevant to repair effectiveness are those that disrupt the bond or composite action. The evidence points to debonding, delamination, and interface failure as the main concerns [N4-R4]. In marine contexts, long-term performance can also be affected by increasing temperatures, which can degrade the elastic modulus and strength of FRP and reduce structural performance [N4-R3]. So, repair effectiveness depends not just on initial bonding, but on the ability to maintain that bond and composite action over time.

---

## 2. How marine environments degrade FRP and what mitigates that degradation

Marine environments degrade FRP primarily through seawater exposure, chloride ingress, biofouling, temperature changes, and hydrostatic pressure. The evidence states that moisture absorption and corrosion are the most significant issues for FRP in marine environments, and that corrosive ions penetrate along with water molecules, causing varying degrees of corrosion to the resin, fibers, and interfaces [N2-F1]. Biofouling is also important, with FRP showing reduced biofouling due to its smooth, low-energy surface that discourages microorganism and marine life adhesion [N2-R1]. This means marine degradation is not only chemical but also biological, and FRP’s performance can be compromised by both wetting and organism growth [N2-R1][N2-F1].

Seawater and chloride exposure are especially relevant. The evidence on seawater effects shows that seawater content and temperature influence the properties of GFRP composites [N2-R2]. The marine dock study notes severe corrosion of steel in submerged reinforced concrete structures, which is a direct environmental driver for using FRP in marine zones [N5-R2]. Although the evidence does not provide a direct degradation model for chloride alone, it clearly establishes that marine exposure generally reduces mechanical properties through water and ion ingress [N2-F1].

Temperature and hydrostatic pressure are also important. Increasing temperatures can degrade the elastic modulus and strength of FRP, leading to reduced structural performance [N4-R3]. Hydrostatic pressure is less directly addressed in the provided evidence, but it is an implicit concern in underwater environments. The underwater repair paper notes that bond strength is greatly affected by casting and curing conditions, and that underwater-cast specimens show much higher bond strength than dry-cast specimens [N3-F2]. This suggests that immersion-related conditions can alter how the FRP system develops strength, even though the evidence does not quantify the pressure effect explicitly [N3-F2].

To mitigate marine degradation, surface treatments and coatings are important. The evidence on adhesively bonded FRP/steel joints notes that the stability of interfacial adhesion in the presence of moisture is the most important factor in long-term durability [N6-R1]. This supports the use of coatings to protect the interface and reduce moisture ingress. Urethane coatings are noted for good chemical resistance and excellent resistance to UV light, making them suitable for marine contexts [N6-R2]. Adhesion force between FRP and coatings is also related to the roughness and wettability of the FRP surface, with the highest adhesion achieved when the glass surface is optimized [N6-R4]. This means that coatings can improve marine resistance, but only if the surface is properly prepared to achieve good wettability and adhesion [N6-R4][N6-R2]. The evidence also highlights that FRP’s resistance to saltwater corrosion and long-term durability make it attractive for marine applications [N6-R5], reinforcing the idea that coatings and surface treatments are complementary to the material’s inherent corrosion resistance.

---

## 3. How underwater and marine repair systems are installed and maintained

Underwater and marine repair systems require special installation methods because the wet environment complicates access, adhesion, and curing. The evidence shows that underwater repair is usually difficult work requiring specialized materials and installation systems [N3-F2]. A proposed TRC grouting system uses a carbon-textile-reinforced concrete grout and evaluates installation methods through bi-surface shear tests [N3-F2]. The paper also describes that grout can be filled through gravity flow if it has high workability, and that textile grids or fabrics can be used to prevent grout from escaping voids [N3-F2]. This suggests that wet-environment repair relies on methods that minimize leakage, control placement, and allow the repair material to set properly even when submerged.

Access management is a major issue in marine zones. For smaller damaged areas, forms or jackets are installed over the section to be repaired, and cementitious grouts are then pumped in [N3-F2]. For underwater repair, removable forms and jackets such as plywood forms and steel jackets are common [N3-F2]. This implies that access is often managed by enclosing the repair zone in temporary containment, so that grout or repair material can be introduced without interference from currents or wave action. The evidence also emphasizes that installation methods can vary depending on the size of the damaged area and the accessibility of the structure [N3-F2]. In practical terms, this means that underwater repair often depends on site-specific solutions such as cofferdams, jackets, or grouting systems rather than generic methods.

In wet environments, adhesion and curing must be managed carefully. FRP-to-concrete bonding in EBFRP systems relies on strong adhesive bonding for effective stress transfer [N1-R2], and the FRP laminate is bonded using an epoxy adhesive that must cure fully [N1-R4]. The underwater repair paper notes that bond strength can be greatly affected by casting and curing conditions, especially when materials are exposed to underwater conditions rather than dry conditions [N3-F2]. It also reports that the use of non-dispersive, anti-washout grouts reduces the difference in bond strength across curing conditions [N3-F2]. This indicates that in marine repair, curing is often managed by selecting materials and installation sequences that minimize washout and allow proper bonding and hardening.

Recommended maintenance and inspection practices are implied by the need to monitor performance over time. The evidence repeatedly stresses the importance of failure analysis in extending the lifespan of FRP systems [N4-R4], which suggests that regular inspection and monitoring are necessary to detect early signs of bond degradation, debonding, or other failure mechanisms. Although the provided evidence does not give a detailed maintenance schedule, it does indicate that the repair system’s long-term effectiveness depends on preserving the bond and preventing premature failure [N4-R4]. In practice, this likely means inspection of the repaired zone for cracks, delamination, and changes in bond appearance, combined with periodic testing if feasible [N3-F2][N4-R4].

---

## 4. Evidence from real-world applications and limitations

Real-world applications of FRP in marine concrete structures are documented in the case-study evidence. The Florida bridges and structures report highlights recent applications of FRP in new construction, including Basalt-FRP and Glass-FRP reinforcing bars for concrete bridge structures, Carbon-FRP prestressed bridge beams, FRP structural shapes, and pilings [N5-F3]. It also notes that FRP has been used in non-bridge applications such as precast and cast-in-place retaining walls, seawalls, and thermoset piling and structural shape elements for in-water structures [N5-F3]. These examples show that FRP is being used not only for strengthening existing structures but also as part of new marine infrastructure design.

The reported performance gains in practice are related to durability, extended service life, and corrosion resistance. The Florida case-study evidence emphasizes that FRP is used because it addresses corrosion durability concerns and supports extended service life [N5-F3]. It also states that Florida has a long coastline and that FRP’s value proposition includes durability versus cost, extended service life versus cost, and reliability versus cost [N5-F3]. This implies that the main reported benefit is that FRP can reduce the need for frequent repairs and replacement in marine environments, thereby lowering life-cycle costs [N5-F3]. The evidence also mentions that FRP applications in new construction have been supported by authoritative resources, guidelines, and specifications, including AASHTO and CSA standards [N5-F3]. This suggests that the practical advantages of FRP include standardized deployment and confidence in performance under marine conditions.

However, the evidence also reveals observed issues and limitations. First, the marine dock study notes that severe corrosion of steel can occur in submerged portions of reinforced concrete structures in marine environments, which highlights the need for alternative materials in such zones [N5-R2]. This implies that while FRP is corrosion-resistant, conventional steel reinforcement in submerged concrete is still vulnerable, and FRP is used as a replacement in those zones [N5-R2]. Second, the underwater repair paper notes that FRPs are only viable for underwater repair in some circumstances and that new techniques must be established to handle the unfavorable conditions of underwater work [N3-R3]. This indicates that FRP is not universally applicable underwater and that special installation techniques are required to make it effective [N3-R3]. Third, the evidence on marine durability notes that moisture absorption and corrosion can significantly reduce the mechanical properties of FRP-like materials, and that long-term life prediction methods remain uncertain [N2-F1]. This suggests that even though FRP is durable, its performance in marine environments can still degrade over time, and the exact rate and extent of degradation are not fully predictable [N2-F1].

The evidence does not provide a direct list of “where FRP is not suitable,” but it implies that suitability depends on the environment and the repair method. The underwater repair paper explicitly states that FRPs are only viable for underwater repair under certain conditions, and that new techniques must be established to handle unfavorable conditions [N3-R3]. The marine dock study further implies that in submerged steel-reinforced concrete, the problem is severe corrosion of steel, so FRP is used as a substitute where steel would otherwise corrode [N5-R2]. In other words, FRP is less suitable for environments where steel reinforcement is not being replaced or where the repair method cannot accommodate special installation and curing requirements [N3-R3][N5-R2]. Overall, the real-world evidence supports FRP as a viable marine repair material, but only when corrosion resistance, proper installation, and long-term durability are explicitly managed [N5-F3][N5-R2][N3-R3].

The underwater repair context further shows that installation methods must be specially established to minimize unfavorable conditions, including those that interfere with adhesion [N3-R3]. In practice, this likely means that wet repair systems need waterproofing, controlled curing, and methods to prevent contamination of the adhesive interface [N3-F2][N3-R3].

This suggests that sealants can improve durability if they are chemically compatible with FRP and if the surface is prepared to promote wettability [N6-R2][N6-R4]. In marine repair, such coatings may act as a barrier against seawater, biofouling, and corrosion, thereby preserving the bond and extending the service life of the FRP system [N2-R1][N6-R2].

Surface preparation is therefore a key determinant of long-term performance. The evidence on adhesion between FRP and coatings indicates that roughness and wettability affect adhesion [N6-R4], which means that improper surface preparation can lead to weak or unreliable bonds. The underwater repair context also shows that the bond strength depends on casting and curing conditions, implying that the repair surface must be properly conditioned before installation [N3-F2]. In marine zones, surface preparation likely includes cleaning, drying, and applying primers or sealants to ensure good wettability and adhesion [N6-R4][N3-F2]. Poor surface preparation can make the repair ineffective because the FRP may not bond well to the concrete, leading to premature debonding or loss of load transfer [N1-R2][N6-R4].
